chunks: "Bus capacitance is basically a sum, so anything I add to the line or change about the geometry moves it.
The biggest contributors are the devices: each pin is a few pF, more if there's a big ESD structure or a mux.

Next is the PCB trace: it scales with length, and with the geometry, so a wider trace, a thinner dielectric to the ground plane, or a higher r all increase it, roughly 1 picofarads per cm for a typical 50 ohms trace.
Then connectors and cables, which can add tens of pF per metre and are often the dominant term on a modular system. It also changes at run time.
If I hot-plug a module, switch an I2C mux channel, or power a device up or down, the capacitance seen on the bus changes.
Junction capacitance depends on voltage, so a pin looks a bit different at 3. 3 volts than at 0 volts.
So to control it I shorten traces, keep the layout tight, choose low-capacitance ESD parts, isolate unused branches with a mux or buffer, and then measure the rise time on a scope to confirm.
I'd also add margin, because the number that matters is the worst case, not the nominal."
